title: OpenAI expands free ChatGPT access to 200,000 researchers and adds 50,000 new grants
summary: If you’re doing research and hesitating over a ChatGPT subscription: OpenAI is expanding free research access to up to 200,000 researchers worldwide, and the next round of 50,000 grants opens November 23 on a first-come, first-served basis.
ai_summary: OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers from a small July pilot into a free program for up to 200,000 researchers worldwide. The next round opens November 23 with 50,000 grants, first come, first served. Each grant covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, so this round could reach up to 150,000 people. Two changes from the pilot: selection moves from a lottery to first come, first served, and the free subscription switches from ChatGPT Pro to Plus, because OpenAI says most participants would have stayed within Plus limits. By default, data shared through the program isn’t used to train models. It’s aimed at researchers who want to apply frontier models to their work without tracking subscription costs; the announcement doesn’t give regular Plus pricing or detailed eligibility criteria.
brief: The new round offers 50,000 free grants, first come, first served from November 23 — no more lottery.
Each grant covers the recipient plus up to two collaborators, so this round can reach up to 150,000 researchers.
The free subscription switches from ChatGPT Pro to ChatGPT Plus; by default, data shared through the program isn’t used to train models.
The pilot has brought in 20,000 researchers across 33 countries; participants estimated the same research work would take nearly twice as long without AI.

sections.h: What this is: OpenAI expands free ChatGPT access for researchers from a pilot to a larger program

blocks.p: On November 16, 2026, OpenAI announced the expansion of ChatGPT for Academic Researchers. In short, it gives eligible researchers free access to ChatGPT so they can apply frontier models to their work without being shut out by subscription fees. The program ran as a small pilot in July and now moves into a larger round.

sections.h: How to apply in the new round: first come, first served, each grant covers you and up to two collaborators

blocks.p: Applications open Monday, November 23. The biggest change from the pilot: no lottery. Instead, the first 50,000 eligible applications get a grant. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, OpenAI will email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

fig.title: Three changes between the pilot and this round
fig.subtitle: Amber marks what changes this round; the neutral color marks the pilot approach; gray marks what the announcement doesn’t say.
fig.footer: First come, first served means applying as soon as you're eligible is the safer bet; it’s no longer down to luck.

blocks.p: Each grant gives the recipient plus up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. That makes this round’s ceiling 150,000 researchers — 50,000 grants, each covering up to two additional people.

callout.title: 150,000 is the ceiling, not a guarantee
callout.text: The total reaches 150,000 only if every grant includes both collaborators; the actual number depends on how many people each grant covers.

sections.h: Why OpenAI replaced free ChatGPT Pro with Plus

blocks.p: The pilot gave researchers ChatGPT Pro, the pricier tier with higher limits and more compute. After reviewing pilot usage, OpenAI says most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus limits, so this round offers Plus to extend access to more research teams.

callout.title: Good enough for most projects — but watch out for heavy compute
callout.text: If your research needs long-running, large-scale compute, Plus limits may be tighter than Pro. The announcement doesn’t specify limits for either tier, so they can’t be compared directly.

sections.h: Pilot results: 20,000 researchers in 33 countries, saving nearly half the time

blocks.p: Since the pilot began in July, 20,000 researchers across 33 countries have joined. OpenAI’s Economic Research team has published Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, a study of more than 1,800 pilot participants.
One notable number: respondents estimated that without AI, doing the same research at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

callout.title: How to read that 'nearly twice as long' figure
callout.text: It’s a self-estimate from survey respondents, not a controlled experiment, so treat it with some caution.

sections.h: What researchers actually use ChatGPT for

blocks.p: The pilot surfaced two public examples: one in medicine and one in biodiversity.

fig.title: Pilot use cases: from drug targets to museum specimens
fig.subtitle: Cards show research examples mentioned in the announcement, plus one general program benefit.

items.title: Finding new drug targets
items.desc: Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, is exploring whether ChatGPT can connect lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development, with one goal being to shorten tuberculosis treatment.

items.title: Turning specimen photos into databases
items.desc: Arthur Porto’s team at the Florida Museum of Natural History uses AI to turn museum specimen photos into searchable databases, and created a 3D butterfly model whose wings change color as you turn it.

items.title: Frontier models + training
items.desc: Participants get access to OpenAI’s frontier models and training on how to use ChatGPT in their research.

sections.h: Beyond this program, what other access do researchers have?

blocks.p: ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one route. OpenAI also offers ChatGPT Edu for universities, covering research, teaching, and learning with data analysis tools and administrative controls, and GPT-Rosalind for biology research, which combines specialized biological reasoning with access to scientific tools and databases.

blocks.p: The Rosalind Academic Plan gives eligible U.S. university labs up to 30 free seats for up to 12 months, but accessing GPT-Rosalind first requires going through a trusted-access approval process.
In mathematics, OpenAI contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

sections.h: Pricing and privacy: how free is it, and will your data be used to train models?

blocks.p: On price: this round is a free grant of ChatGPT Plus, and the 50,000 grants themselves cost nothing. But the announcement doesn’t give the regular ChatGPT Plus subscription price or the pilot-period ChatGPT Pro price, so you can’t calculate exactly how much you’re saving.
On privacy: by default, OpenAI doesn’t use data shared through the program to train its models. That’s the default setting — the announcement doesn’t spell out exceptions.

list: The regular price of ChatGPT Plus and the pilot-period ChatGPT Pro price: not stated.
The exact meaning of 'eligible': the announcement says applications must be eligible but doesn’t list detailed criteria.
How long the 50,000 grants are expected to last, or how they’re distributed across countries: not stated.
Whether researchers who got Pro during the pilot will be automatically renewed or downgraded in this round: not stated.
The application deadline: the announcement only says applications open November 23, with no closing date.
Whether there are exceptions or options beyond 'not trained by default': not stated.

blocks.p: The value is straightforward: eligible researchers, plus up to two collaborators, get free ChatGPT Plus for their work, with training included and a default guarantee that your data isn’t used to train models. The tradeoff is that it’s only ChatGPT Plus — which may be tight for heavy compute — and you have to claim a grant before they run out.

list: If your project involves lots of literature searching, coding, data cleaning, or paper drafting, and your team is no larger than you plus two collaborators, apply as early as possible in this round.
If you’re on the waitlist, check your inbox: eligible researchers will get activation instructions before applications open.
If you’re a biology lab at a U.S. university, look at the Rosalind Academic Plan’s 30 free seats as well.
If you need long-running, large-scale compute, first confirm that Plus limits will be enough — the announcement doesn’t give specific limits.
